definition.text: Disaster recovery is the process of regaining access to infrastructure and systems after a natural disaster, cyber attack or other business disruption.

facts.text: Disaster recovery relies on replicating data and computer processing to an off-premises location that the disaster does not affect.
It assumes the primary site cannot be recovered right away, so it restores data and services to a secondary site.
When servers go down, the business recovers lost data from a second location where it is backed up and, ideally, moves its processing there to keep operating.
Disaster recovery applies policies, tools and procedures to the IT systems behind critical business functions, and is a subset of business continuity.

Disasters come from three broad categories: natural hazards such as floods and earthquakes, technological hazards such as system failures and utility disruptions, and human-caused threats such as cyber attacks, sabotage and war.
Disaster recovery minimizes interruption and downtime, limits damage, speeds restoration and helps retain customers.

Regulators mandate disaster recovery for organizations handling sensitive data; in US healthcare the HIPAA Security Rule requires disaster recovery plans, data backup plans and periodic testing of contingency procedures.
Singh notes that disaster recovery is seldom discussed in system design interviews but is worth a basic understanding.

title: Recovery time objective
article: IT disaster recovery#IT service continuity > Recovery Time Objective

definition.text: The recovery time objective (RTO) is the maximum acceptable delay between an interruption of service and its restoration.

facts.text: The RTO sets the acceptable window during which a service may be unavailable, that is, how long an application or network can stay offline after a disaster.
In business continuity planning the process owners set the RTO during a business impact analysis, including time frames for alternate or manual workarounds.
The business continuity group runs timed rehearsals to determine and refine the recovery time actual (RTA), the critical metric against which the RTO is checked.
RTO and RPO together measure tolerable performance: time lost from normal business functioning, and data lost or not backed up during that period.
RTO and RPO must be balanced against business risk and the other system design criteria.
Recovery metrics are often used alongside failure metrics: mean time between failures, mean time to first failure, mean time to repair and mean down time.

title: Recovery point objective
article: IT disaster recovery#IT service continuity > Recovery Point Objective

definition.text: The recovery point objective (RPO) is the maximum acceptable amount of time since the last recovery point, that is, the longest interval of data loss tolerated.

facts.text: The RPO fixes what counts as an acceptable loss of data between the last recovery point and the interruption of service.
RPO measures the maximum time in which recent data might be permanently lost, not the quantity of data lost.
If the plan is to restore the last available backup, the RPO is the interval between such backups.
The existing backup regime does not determine the RPO; the business impact analysis determines it for each service.
When the RPO is measured in minutes, off-site mirrored backups must be maintained continuously, because a daily off-site backup will not suffice.
When data must go off-site, the period in which data might be lost may start when backups are prepared, not when they are secured off-site.
A data synchronization point is where a backup is completed; update processing halts during the disk-to-disk copy, and the backup reflects the data as of that copy, not when it reaches tape.
Sending synchronous copies to an offsite mirror allows for most unforeseen events.

definition.text: A disaster recovery strategy is the set of measures chosen to restore systems and data after a disaster, derived from the business continuity plan.

facts.text: The strategy derives from the business continuity plan; a cost-benefit analysis picks the measures, since the right one depends on the cost of downtime compared with the cost of implementing it.
Common strategies are backups to tape sent off-site, backups to disk on-site and copied off-site, and replication off-site; storing data off-site or on a removable drive is the simplest.

Cloud options include private cloud replication of metadata, hybrid cloud replication both on-site and off-site for instant fail-over, high availability systems replicated off-site, and disaster recovery as a service from a third-party vendor.
Precautionary measures include local mirrors and RAID, surge protectors, an uninterruptible power supply or backup generator, fire prevention systems and anti-virus software.

title: Hot, warm and cold sites
article: IT disaster recovery#IT service continuity > Principles of backup sites

definition.text: A backup site is hot if it operates before a disaster, warm if it is ready to begin operating, and cold if it needs substantial work to begin operating.

facts.text: A robust disaster recovery strategy starts from two benchmarks, the recovery time objective and the recovery point objective, and picks a standby tier that meets them.
In a cold site the organization sets up only basic infrastructure in a second site.
A hot site keeps up-to-date copies of data at all times; it is time-consuming to set up and costs more than a cold site, but dramatically reduces downtime.
Backup and restore means regular backups of data and systems; typical RTO runs from several hours to a few days, and RPO from a few hours up to the last successful backup.
Pilot light keeps crucial components ready to activate so it can scale rapidly; typical RTO is a few minutes to several hours, and RPO depends on how often data is synchronized.
Warm standby is a semi-active environment with current data; typical RTO is within a few minutes to hours, and RPO is up to the last few minutes or hours.

A hot site or multi-site configuration is a fully operational duplicate environment running in parallel with the primary; typical RTO is almost immediate, often a few minutes, and RPO is usually a few seconds.

notes: The article anchor covers hot/warm/cold; the four tiers (backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, multi-site) come from the ByteByteGo cloud-disaster-recovery-strategies guide.

definition.text: Disaster recovery practices are the controls, tests and procedures that keep a recovery plan working when a disaster happens.

facts.text: Controls are preventive, detective or corrective, are recorded in the disaster recovery plan, and are exercised regularly in DR tests that verify the plan and expose weaknesses or gaps.
A cloud recovery strategy should be flexible enough for partial failures, such as recovering specific files, as well as for full environment failures.
Define who may execute the plan and separate those permissions from access to backup data, which limits unauthorized actions; document the plan so operators can follow it under stress.
Planning ahead is cost-effective: every $1 spent on hazard mitigation, such as a disaster recovery plan, saves society $4 in response and recovery costs.

definition.text: High availability architectures pair a node with a standby, secondary or second primary so the service keeps answering when one node fails.

facts.text: In the CAP theorem, availability means every non-failing node can be queried and returns a reasonable response within a reasonable time, with no error or timeout.
A design target of 4-9's means the service is up 99.99% of the time and down at most 52.5 minutes per year.
Availability only guarantees a response, not that the data is the most up-to-date.
In primary-backup, the backup is a stand-by that receives replicated data; on failure the switch to it is manual, and the idle backup may waste hardware.
In primary-secondary, the secondary can serve reads to balance load, but replication latency means reads from it may be inconsistent with the primary.

In primary-primary, both nodes handle reads and writes and replicate to each other, raising throughput; but if both update the same product the final state can be unpredictable, so use it with caution.
Deploying on Amazon EC2, which has 90% availability, a double-node architecture raises availability from 90% to 99%.

definition.text: Observability is the ability to ask arbitrary questions about a system without knowing ahead of time what to ask; logging, tracing and metrics are its three pillars.

facts.text: Logging records discrete events, such as an incoming request or a visit to a database, and has the highest volume of the three pillars.
Teams define a standardized logging format so keywords can be searched across massive logs; the ELK (Elastic-Logstash-Kibana) stack is often used to build a log analysis platform.
Tracing is request-scoped: it follows one user request through the API gateway, load balancer, services and database, which helps identify bottlenecks.
Metrics are aggregatable measurements such as service QPS, API responsiveness and latency, with raw data recorded in time-series databases like InfluxDB.
Prometheus pulls the metrics and transforms them by pre-defined alerting rules; Grafana displays them, and the alert manager sends email, SMS or Slack notifications.
OpenTelemetry unifies the three pillars in a single framework.

definition.text: A service level indicator (SLI) is a measure of the service level a provider delivers to a customer.

facts.text: SLIs form the basis of service level objectives, which in turn form the basis of service level agreements; an SLI is also called an SLA metric or service metric.
An SLI is the measured value of the metric an SLO describes; to stay in compliance with the SLA, its value must always meet or exceed the SLO's value.
Common SLIs are latency, throughput, availability and error rate; others include durability for storage systems, end-to-end latency for pipelines, and correctness.
The availability SLI varies with the service's nature and architecture; a simple web service might use the ratio of successful responses to the total valid requests received.

definition.text: A service-level agreement (SLA) is an agreement, typically a binding contract, between a service provider and a customer that sets the quality, availability and responsibilities of a service as contract terms.

facts.text: An SLA defines the promises a company makes to its users about specific metrics such as service availability, and is often written by the company's business or legal team.

SLAs often contain service-level objectives for defined service level indicators, such as mean time between failures, mean time to repair, network throughput, jitter, uptime, first-call resolution and turnaround time.
SLAs, SLOs and SLIs let companies define, track and monitor their promises to users, which builds user trust and drives continuous improvement of incident response.
Unlike traditional contracts, SLAs often require the parties to meet regularly, apply rewards and penalties for performance, and leave room for periodic revision.

Large organizations keep internal SLAs between units, one as customer and one as provider, which keeps quality of service consistent across units and locations and allows comparing an in-house department with an external provider.

SLAs exist at different levels: customer-based for one customer group across all its services, service-based for all customers of a service, and multilevel when one SLA addresses different customer sets in layers.
In outsourcing, SLAs are negotiated upfront in the contract, which may carry financial penalties and a right to terminate if SLA metrics are consistently missed.
SLAs may be supported by operational-level agreements (OLAs).

title: SLA components

definition.text: A well-defined SLA contains the type of service, the desired performance level, monitoring and reporting, steps for reporting issues, response and resolution time frames, and repercussions for missed commitments.

facts.text: It names the type of service and the desired performance level, especially reliability (minimal disruption, available almost always) and responsiveness (acting promptly after a request).
It describes how performance is monitored: which statistics are gathered, how often, and how customers can access them.
It gives contact details and the order for reporting a problem; the response time frame is when the provider starts investigating, and the resolution time frame is when the issue is fixed.
If the provider misses its commitments, the customer may have the right to terminate the contract or ask for a refund for losses from the service failure.

notes: Components follow Dinesh Verma's list as given in the Wikipedia section.

definition.text: Cloud SLAs are service-based agreements that cover a shared infrastructure rather than agreements with one customer.

facts.text: Because cloud resources are shared, SLAs span the cloud and are offered by providers as service-based rather than customer-based agreements.

Cloud performance is measured and reported from the end user's ability to consume resources; cloud SLAs focus on data center characteristics and, more recently, network characteristics to support end-to-end SLAs.

The downside of the cloud is that the complex environment makes the root cause of service interruptions hard to determine, yet applications moved there must reach the same or more demanding service levels.
Any SLA management strategy has two phases: negotiating the contract and monitoring its fulfillment in real time.

definition.text: A service-level objective (SLO) is a target value or range of values for a service level, measured by a service level indicator.

facts.text: An SLO is a key element of an SLA, an individual promise within it, and the specific goal the service must meet to comply; typical SLOs cover availability, throughput, frequency, response time or quality.
SLOs give a quantitative definition of the service level a customer can expect, and are agreed to measure the provider's performance and avoid disputes from misunderstanding.
In simple terms, SLOs are targets for how often a service may fail or not operate properly while users are still not meaningfully upset.
SLOs are formed by setting goals for SLIs; an availability SLO may be the expected value of an availability SLI over a prescribed duration, for example four weeks.
An SLO should state an achievement value, a target measurement, a measurement period, and where and how it is measured, for example 90% of helpdesk calls answered in under 20 seconds over one month.
Example SLOs include an application available 99.95% of the time over a year, and 85% of TCP replies within 1.5 seconds and 99.5% within 4 seconds over a month.
SLOs should always be simple, clearly defined and easy to measure, so it is clear whether the objective is being met.
Companies may also set internal SLOs for internal services that depend on each other, especially those practicing site reliability engineering.

definition.text: Site reliability engineering (SRE) is a discipline that applies software engineering to IT infrastructure and operations to monitor and improve the availability and performance of deployed software systems.

facts.text: SREs are responsible for a combination of availability, latency, performance, efficiency, change management, monitoring, emergency response and capacity planning.
SRE focuses on automation, system design and improved resilience, typically with an infrastructure as code methodology.
SRE is considered a specific implementation of DevOps that concentrates on building reliable systems, while DevOps covers a broader scope of operations.

Common practices include automating repetitive tasks, defining reliability goals to prevent endless effort, designing systems to reduce risks to availability, latency and efficiency, and observability.
Toil management is a principle: toil is manual, repetitive, automatable operational work.
Reliability goals are defined and measured with SLIs, SLOs and error budgets.
Other principles are defining, testing and running an incident management process, and change and release management including CI/CD.

definition.text: SRE teams are organized in several models: kitchen sink, infrastructure, product or application, embedded and consulting.

facts.text: A kitchen sink team oversees an expansive, often unbounded scope, including performance optimization, incident management and automation.
Infrastructure SRE teams keep the systems that support other teams' workflows up, fast and efficient, while platform teams develop the software and systems used across the organization.
Product or application SRE teams are dedicated to specific products, and large companies typically have several, each focusing on different products or applications.

In the embedded model, individual SREs or pairs join software engineering teams to apply automation, monitoring and incident response; consulting SRE teams instead advise organizations on adopting SRE practices.
